analysis.one_liner: Makes the federal government meet a higher burden of proof before taking property in civil forfeiture and stops it from keeping the proceeds.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the bar for federal civil asset forfeiture never got a hearing or a vote and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it harder for the federal government to take people's property without charging them with a crime. In civil forfeiture cases, the government now only needs a preponderance of the evidence and can take property even when the owner played no role in any offense; the bill would require clear and convincing evidence that the owner knowingly used the property in connection with a crime. It would also stop forfeited money from going directly into Department of Justice accounts and send it to the Treasury instead, removing the financial incentive agencies have to seize property.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose property the federal government seizes in a civil forfeiture case — including people never charged with a crime — would gain stronger protection: the government would have to prove its case with clear and convincing evidence and show the owner knowingly connected the property to a crime, and forfeited money would no longer flow directly into law enforcement budgets.

how_it_helps.text: It raises the government's burden of proof in civil forfeiture from a preponderance of the evidence to clear and convincing evidence, making it harder to take property on thin grounds.

It requires the government to prove the owner of seized property actually used it in connection with an offense or knowingly allowed it — closing the practice of seizing property from owners who took no part in any crime.
It routes forfeited money to the Treasury's General Fund instead of Department of Justice accounts, removing the direct financial incentive for agencies to seize property.
The changes would apply immediately to any civil forfeiture case pending on or after enactment, not just future cases.

analysis.who_pays: Federal law enforcement agencies would bear the cost: they would lose forfeited property as direct revenue for their own budgets and face a harder legal standard for taking property in civil cases.

drawbacks.text: Raising the standard to clear and convincing evidence would make it harder for the government to strip drug traffickers and criminal organizations of their proceeds, assets that currently fund law enforcement work.
Ending the direct flow of forfeiture proceeds to the Department of Justice would take money out of police and prosecutor budgets unless Congress appropriated replacement funds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — protecting innocent owners from losing cash, cars, and homes without a criminal conviction — is significant, since under the current preponderance standard the government can keep property without proving the owner did anything wrong. The honest cost is that the higher standard and owner-culpability requirement would also slow legitimate seizures of criminal proceeds, and law enforcement agencies would lose a funding stream they currently control. The bill does not appropriate replacement funds, so the budget hit to law enforcement would be real.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in subcommittees of the Judiciary and Energy and Commerce Committees until Congress ended in January 2015, and the House never voted on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 17, 2014, with one Republican and one Democratic cosponsor, and referred to the House Judiciary and Energy and Commerce Committees.
In its first six weeks it was referred twice more — to the Health subcommittee on September 19 and the Crime subcommittee on October 28 — and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
The bill never reached the House floor, and Congress adjourned on January 3, 2015, ending the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal law enforcement agencies are better off: the existing rules — a low burden of proof for civil seizures and forfeited funds flowing straight into Department of Justice accounts — remained in place. Property owners facing civil forfeiture gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal law enforcement agencies kept the old rules

for.name: Rep. Scott Garrett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FAIR Act to raise the burden of proof in civil forfeiture and end DOJ's direct use of forfeited funds.

against.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee and then to its Crime subcommittee, where no markup or vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; sponsorship was nominally bipartisan, with a Republican sponsor joined by one Republican and one Democratic cosponsor.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement agencies (Department of Justice, DEA, FBI)
industries.note: Forfeiture proceeds currently go into DOJ accounts for law enforcement activities [S2]; the bill would redirect them to the Treasury's General Fund and raise the standard for seizing property. Agencies would lose both a revenue stream tied to seizures and an easy legal path to taking property.
